## Exploring the Iris Dataset

In this analysis, I explore the Iris dataset using Python. The goal is to examine the characteristics of the different Iris species and visualize patterns in the data.

Data: [Iris dataset from scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.datasets.load_iris.html), originally introduced by R. A. Fisher.

```{python}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

## Loading the Data

```{python}
iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
df = iris.frame
df.head()
```

## Sepal Length by Species

```{python}

#| label: fig-sepal-length
#| fig-cap: "Sepal length distribution for the three Iris species"

df["species"] = df["target"].map(dict(enumerate(iris.target_names)))

df.boxplot(column="sepal length (cm)", by="species")
plt.suptitle("")
plt.title("Sepal Length by Iris Species")
plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Sepal Length (cm)")
plt.show()
```

### Interpretation

The boxplot shows clear differences in sepal length among the three Iris species. Setosa generally has the shortest sepal lengths, virginica has the longest, and versicolor falls between the two. There is some overlap between the distributions, particularly between versicolor and virginica.

## Petal Length vs Petal Width

```{python}
df.plot.scatter(
    x="petal length (cm)",
    y="petal width (cm)",
    c="target",
    colormap="viridis"
)
plt.title("Petal Length vs Petal Width")
plt.show()
```

### Interpretation

The scatter plot shows a strong positive relationship between petal length and petal width. The three Iris species also form distinct clusters, suggesting that petal measurements are useful for distinguishing between species.
